conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to check in on how things are feeling for you since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the EPDS—short for the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s just ten questions about the past week, and it helps us spot anything from normal new-mom overwhelm to signs of depression or anxiety so we can give you the right support. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger. We’ll go at your pace, and you can pause any time. Ready to start?  

First, I’d love to know: over the past seven days, have you still been able to look forward to things you normally enjoy, or has the joy felt a bit dimmed?

*shifts in chair, eyes fixed on the floor*

I... I mean, I *try* to feel excited about stuff. Like yesterday my sister brought over those cinnamon rolls I used to love, and I ate one but... it just tasted like cardboard. My husband texted me a funny meme this morning and I just stared at it. 

*voice cracks slightly*

The only thing that gives me even a tiny spark is when my baby girl smiles at me during tummy time, but even then, this heavy feeling doesn't really go away. It's like I'm watching myself from behind glass - I *know* I should be happy about things, but it's like the color's been drained out of everything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shrugs weakly, eyes still on my lap*

Not really… I mean, I *can* laugh, but it feels forced. My partner tried to joke about the diaper explosions and I gave a little laugh, but it faded right away and I felt guilty for even that. Most of the time I just feel too tired or flat to find anything funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shakes head slowly*

Honestly? Not much... I keep telling myself I *should* be excited about little things—like the new season of that show we used to binge, or even just going for a walk with the stroller. But when I think about doing any of it, it just feels... pointless. Like, why bother? I’ll probably still feel this same heaviness even if I do it. The only thing I kind of look forward to is when my baby sleeps longer stretches at night, because then maybe I could close my eyes for a bit without that anxious knot in my chest.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*voice drops, fingers tightening around the hem of my sweater*

Yeah... a lot. Yesterday she wouldn't nap and just cried, and I kept thinking it must be something I did—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I'm not holding her right, or I'm just... failing her somehow. 

*eyes well up*

When her diaper leaked all over the crib at 3 a.m., the first thing I thought was, "Of course, because I didn't put it on tight enough—I'm terrible at this." Even tiny things, like spilling a little pumped milk, I feel like I'm wasting her food and I'm the worst mom. My brain keeps telling me she deserves someone better than me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*nods quickly, knees bouncing*

All the time. Like, I’ll be feeding her and suddenly I’m sure the latch is wrong and she’s not getting enough milk—even though the pediatrician says she’s gaining fine. Or I’ll lie down and hear a car door outside and my brain jumps to “someone’s going to break in and I won’t be able to protect her.” 

*wrings hands*

Last night I checked the thermostat four times because I was terrified she’d overheat. There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just spin and spin until my chest feels tight. I *know* it’s probably irrational, but I can’t make it stop.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*breath catches*

Yeah... it hits out of nowhere. Like yesterday afternoon—nothing special was happening, she was just napping in the bassinet—but all of a sudden my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn't get enough air. I had to grip the couch cushions to stop myself from shaking. 

*voice trembles*

Sometimes it's so bad I think I'm having a heart attack. It passes after a few minutes, but I'm left sweaty and shaky and watching her chest rise and fall because I'm terrified something will happen to her while I'm falling apart. There's no real danger, but in that moment it feels like the world is ending.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhales shakily*

Yes… most days feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. The sink fills with bottles faster than I can wash them, the laundry pile keeps growing, and every time I sit down she needs something else. I start one task, get interrupted, start another, and suddenly it’s 4 p.m. and I haven’t eaten or brushed my teeth. 

*voice drops*

Sometimes I just stare at the mess and cry because it feels impossible to catch up. I keep thinking, “I’m supposed to handle this, but I can’t even handle today.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*nods, eyes red-rimmed*

Yeah… I’ll finally get her down and crawl into bed, but then my brain won’t shut off. I lie there replaying every little thing I did wrong—did I burp her long enough, did I fasten the swaddle too tight, am I already ruining her life? 

*voice cracks*

It takes me forever to drift off, and when I do, I jolt awake at every tiny grunt over the monitor, heart pounding. Even when my partner takes the early shift, I just stare at the ceiling, feeling this heavy sadness that won’t lift. I’m exhausted, but sleep feels impossible.
I have felt sad or miserable

*shoulders sag*

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud parked over me. I’ll be changing her diaper and tears just start leaking out for no clear reason. 

*voice drops to a whisper*

I look at other moms on social media laughing and cuddling their babies, and I think, “Why can’t I feel that happy?” I keep waiting for the joyful, glowy new-mom feeling everyone promised, but mostly I just feel empty and weepy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods slowly, eyes filling*

Yeah… it’s like the tears are always right there, ready. Yesterday I cried when the pacifier fell on the floor—just sat on the carpet holding it and sobbed like it was the worst thing in the world. 

*voice breaks*

And sometimes I’ll be feeding her and look down and realize my tears are dripping onto her blanket. I feel so guilty for crying around her, but I can’t always stop it. It’s not just once or twice—it’s almost every day now.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*quiet for a long moment, twisting the edge of my sleeve*

…Sometimes, yeah. Not that I want to die or anything—I could never leave her—but when she’s been screaming for an hour and nothing helps, I’ll picture myself running a bath and just… sinking under. 

*voice barely audible*

It flashes in and out, like, “What if I could just turn everything off for five minutes?” I haven’t done anything, I don’t have a plan, but the thought slips in maybe once or twice this week when I feel totally overwhelmed.

You've shared how the joy you once felt has faded since your baby arrived-laughter feels forced, nothing excites you, and a heavy gray cloud hangs over each day. You cry easily, feel overwhelmed by simple tasks, blame yourself when anything goes wrong, and battle constant worry and sudden panic even when everything appears safe. Although you love your daughter dearly, intrusive images of “turning everything off” flash in when the crying won’t stop, leaving you frightened and exhausted yet determined to stay here for her.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 28, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter is rare, forced, and fleeting; mood described as flat and tired, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient expresses anhedonia and anticipates no future pleasure, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive self-blame for routine infant issues, indicating this occurs 'most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes relentless, intrusive worries multiple times daily (feeding, safety, temperature), inability to stop them, and physical tension—clearly maps to "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intense, sudden panic attacks with physical symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness, shaking) occurring without identifiable cause, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to complete basic tasks, tearful staring at mess, and feeling unable to cope "at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing thoughts, anxiety about parenting, and persistent sadness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily crying episodes triggered by minor events, indicating crying "most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly reports intrusive thoughts of self-harm "once or twice this week" during overwhelming moments, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 28 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale places you well above the 14-point cut-off that signals probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> requiring urgent evaluation. Your responses map onto core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: daily depressed mood, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness, fatigue, sleep disruption unrelated to infant care, and recurrent thoughts of death without active plan. You also endorse severe <med>anxiety symptoms</med>-excessive worry, panic attacks, and physiological arousal-commonly co-occurring in postpartum mood disorders. The combination of high EPDS total plus item-10 self-harm ideation (≥1) mandates immediate safety assessment and specialist referral. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to review these results
2. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you and help with baby care until professional support is in place
3. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or go to the nearest ED if self-harm thoughts intensify or you feel unsafe
4. Begin basic self-care: eat small frequent meals, accept offered help, rest when baby rests, limit social media comparisons
5. Discuss medication options and evidence-based therapy such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> with your provider
6. Plan daily 10-minute outdoor stroller walk and simple breathing exercises to gently reduce <sym>anxiety</sym>
7. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track symptom change after starting treatment
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 28: Post-partum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: ___  
Source: Patient self-report (10-item EPDS-style interview)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness nearly daily  
- Marked anhedonia; forced laughter, no anticipatory enjoyment  
- Overwhelming guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Intrusive, irrational worries and panic attacks (cardiac symptoms, hypervigilance about infant safety)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia unrelated to infant demands  
- Frequent crying spells, feeling “empty,” inadequate  
- Sense of being “drowned” by routine tasks, difficulty coping  
- Passive self-harm ideation without intent or plan (30-second intrusive images of “turning off”)

Pattern  
Consistent with moderate–severe postpartum depression with prominent anxiety features. No evidence of hypomania, psychosis, or substance use.

Risk flags  
- Daily sadness, anhedonia, worthlessness  
- Panic-level anxiety, nocturnal rumination  
- Passive suicidal thoughts present; no active plan, intent, or preparatory behavior  
- No protective factors elicited in this screen

Screening impression  
High clinical concern for major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; safety risk warrants immediate follow-up safety assessment and referral for psychiatric evaluation and support services.
